Selincuo naked carp (Schizopygopsis selincuoensis) reaches a maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years] when maintained under the cold, stable thermal regime typical of its high-altitude lacustrine habitat, specifically at a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This longevity, which is considerable for a cyprinid adapted to the oligotrophic waters of the Tibetan Plateau, suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward late maturation and iteroparous reproduction. The species exhibits marked sexual size dimorphism, with females attaining a greater ultimate standard length than males. Field surveys of adult individuals from Selincuo Lake indicate that females reach a maximum standard length of 42 centimeters [Li = 42 centimeters], whereas males are slightly smaller, achieving an ultimate standard length of 38 centimeters [Li = 38 centimeters]. This pattern of female-biased size dimorphism is consistent with observations in several other congeneric Schizopygopsis species and likely reflects the selective advantages of increased fecundity associated with larger body size in females, which allows them to accommodate a greater ovarian mass.

At the onset of independent life, newly emerged yolk-sac larvae of Selincuo naked carp possess a wet weight of approximately 0.00027 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00027 grams], a minute body mass that reflects the small diameter of the demersal eggs from which they hatch. Such a low initial mass, derived from an estimated egg diameter of roughly 0.8 millimeters, positions the neonates among the smallest schizothoracine larvae documented. This modest birth mass imposes a critical energetic constraint: the lecithotrophic yolk-sac larva must rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves for somatic growth and maintenance until the mouth gapes open and the exotrophic transition to first feeding occurs. The finite yolk supply necessitates a relatively brief period of endotrophic development, after which the free-swimming larva must successfully locate and capture prey in the unproductive pelagic zone of the lake. Mortality during this early stage is presumed to be high, consistent with the small body size and limited yolk buffer typical of many cold-water cyprinids.

For adult females, the ultimate asymptotic wet weight reaches 1,100 grams [Wwi = 1,100 grams], a substantial body mass that distinguishes this species from smaller-bodied schizothoracines in the region. In the context of a 10 °C [T = 10 °C] thermal environment, reproductive maturation follows a pronounced sex-specific schedule: females attain puberty at an age of 8 years [tp = 8 years], while males reach sexual maturity more rapidly, becoming reproductively viable at 7 years [tp = 7 years] of age. This approximately 12-month disparity in the timing of the onset of gonadal recrudescence between the sexes is a noteworthy life-history feature. It may reflect differential energetic investment strategies, with females requiring additional time to accumulate the somatic reserves necessary to support the elevated metabolic costs of vitellogenesis and the subsequent production of a large clutch of demersal eggs. Such delayed female maturation is a recurrent pattern observed in iteroparous teleosts inhabiting resource-limited, cold-water ecosystems.

Based on comparative life-history data from the closely related congener Schizopygopsis younghusbandi, scaled to account for the larger ultimate body mass of Selincuo naked carp, the maximum reproductive output at the species' asymptotic size has been estimated. When evaluated at a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], a fully grown female of 1,100 grams [Wwi = 1,100 grams] is inferred to produce approximately 102 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 102 eggs per day]. This daily fecundity, while representing the theoretical maximum at ultimate size, is likely realized only during the peak of the spawning season, which for high-elevation schizothoracines typically coincides with a brief window of elevated summer temperatures. The reproductive strategy is presumably iteroparous, with females spawning annually or perhaps biennially depending on the energetic costs incurred during the preceding growing season. Such a moderate daily egg production rate is consistent with the slow life-history pace imposed by the cold, low-productivity environment.

In its natural lacustrine habitat on the Tibetan Plateau, the life cycle of Schizopygopsis selincuoensis is finely tuned to the pronounced seasonal thermal cycle. Following external fertilisation of the demersal eggs during the brief summer spawning period, the embryonated eggs develop slowly, the yolk-dependent embryos undergoing cleavage, blastula, and gastrulation stages over an extended incubation interval. Hatching typically occurs after the eggs have been incubating for several weeks, releasing a yolk-sac larva that soon begins the process of yolk absorption. The exotrophic transition, marked by first exogenous feeding and the completion of yolk-sac resorption, is a critical bottleneck for larval survival. Thereafter, the actively growing pelagic larva undergoes a gradual larval-juvenile transition involving allometric shifts in body proportions and the onset of fin ray ossification. The protracted period to sexual maturation, with males reaching puberty at 7 years [tp = 7 years] more rapidly than females, underscores the species' position as a slow-growing, long-lived teleost adapted to the extreme oligotrophy and low temperatures of its high-altitude environment at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C].
